lessons.title: Galloping Gertie: Why the Tacoma Narrows Bridge Really Fell
lessons.hook: Generations of physics students have been told that a bridge in Washington State collapsed because the wind hit its resonant frequency. The real explanation is stranger, and far more useful to anyone who designs systems.

sections.heading: An elegant, flexible bridge
sections.body:
When the Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in July 1940, it was the third-longest suspension bridge in the world and a showcase of the era's taste for slender, graceful design. Its designer, Leon Moisseiff, was among the most respected bridge engineers of his day. Instead of the deep steel trusses that normally stiffened a suspension deck, he used shallow plate girders only about 2.4 metres deep. The result was strikingly thin, cheaper to build and, as it turned out, dangerously flexible.

Even during construction, workers noticed that the deck rose and fell in moderate winds. Locals nicknamed it "Galloping Gertie", and some drove across just for the rollercoaster sensation. Engineers added cables and dampers to tame the motion, with limited success.

sections.heading: Four months later
sections.body:
On 7 November 1940, a steady wind of around 65 km/h blew through the Narrows. That morning the motion changed character. Instead of simply rising and falling, the deck began to twist, one edge lifting while the other dropped, so that the roadway tilted dramatically from side to side. The twisting grew for roughly an hour until a long section of the deck tore loose and fell into the water below.

Remarkably, the only fatality was a dog left in a car abandoned on the bridge. The whole sequence was filmed, and the footage remains one of the most famous engineering clips ever recorded.

sections.heading: Not resonance, but flutter
sections.body:
The popular explanation is resonance: the wind supposedly pushed the bridge rhythmically at its natural frequency, like a parent pushing a child on a swing. The trouble is that the wind that day was steady, not pulsing in a regular rhythm, so there was no periodic push to match.

What actually happened is called aeroelastic flutter, and the key idea is feedback. When the thin deck twisted slightly, it changed the way air flowed around it, and that altered airflow pushed the deck further into the twist. The structure's own motion was generating the forces that drove it. Once the wind speed crossed a critical threshold, the energy pumped in on each cycle exceeded what the structure could dissipate, and the oscillation grew until something gave way. Engineers call this a self-excited oscillation, a subtler and more insidious phenomenon than forced resonance.

A useful way to picture it is a flag flapping in a steady breeze. Nobody is shaking the flag rhythmically, yet it keeps rippling, because each movement of the fabric reshapes the airflow, which then pushes the fabric again. The Tacoma deck behaved like an enormous steel flag, except that its flapping put loads on the hangers and girders that they had never been designed to withstand.

sections.heading: What changed afterwards
sections.body:
The collapse ended the fashion for ever-slimmer decks. The official investigation concluded that the bridge had been designed competently for static loads, but its aerodynamic behaviour had never been seriously analysed, partly because no comparable failure had been studied before. From then on, wind-tunnel testing of scale models became standard practice for major bridges, and designers began paying close attention to the shape of a deck's cross-section, not just its strength. The replacement bridge, opened in 1950, used deep, open trusses that let the wind pass through and resisted twisting far better.

Today the second-generation bridge still stands, and a parallel span was added in 2007 to carry the growing traffic.

sections.heading: Why it matters beyond bridges
sections.body:
The deeper lesson is about feedback loops. A system that responds to its environment can, under the wrong conditions, start feeding its own instability. The same pattern appears when a microphone picks up its own loudspeaker and the sound system howls, or when a poorly tuned controller hunts back and forth around its set point instead of settling.

Charging software faces a version of this too. If a load-balancing algorithm reacts too aggressively to measurements that its own decisions produced, power allocations can swing back and forth rather than converge. The remedy is the same in principle as at Tacoma: understand the loop, add damping, and test under realistic conditions instead of trusting a design that only looks good on paper.

lessons.takeaway: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge was not shaken apart by rhythmic gusts; its own motion turned a steady wind into a growing force. Whenever a system reacts to its own effects, look for the feedback loop.

lessons.title: The Steel Box That Shrank the World
lessons.hook: The most important invention in modern trade is not the internet or the jet engine but a plain steel box, and its real breakthrough was not the box itself but the system built around it.

sections.heading: Ports before the box
sections.body:
Until the late 1950s, loading a cargo ship was a slow, labour-intensive craft. Goods arrived at the docks in sacks, barrels, crates and bales of every shape, and gangs of dockworkers carried, hoisted and stowed them piece by piece. A ship could spend almost as long in port being loaded and unloaded as it spent at sea.

Theft was rampant, breakage was common, and handling often made up a large share of the total cost of shipping. For many goods, moving them across an ocean was relatively cheap; moving them across the quay was not.

sections.heading: A trucker's idea
sections.body:
The change came from outside the shipping industry. Malcom McLean was an American trucking entrepreneur who grew frustrated watching his lorries wait for hours at ports. His insight was that the trailer body could be lifted off its wheels and put straight onto a ship, so that the cargo inside would never have to be touched between the factory and the customer. In 1956 he converted a tanker to carry boxes on deck and sent the Ideal X from Newark to Houston with 58 containers on board.

The economics were startling. By most estimates, loading loose cargo at the time cost several dollars per ton, while loading containers cost a small fraction of that, a saving of well over ninety per cent. Ships could turn around in hours instead of days, and goods could travel sealed from origin to destination.

McLean understood that he was not really in the shipping business at all, but in the business of moving freight from door to door. That shift in perspective mattered more than any piece of hardware. He went on to build Sea-Land, one of the first lines designed entirely around containers, and to lobby ports and regulators to accept a model that most of the industry still dismissed as eccentric.

sections.heading: Why it took twenty years
sections.body:
Yet the container did not conquer the world overnight. The box was the easy part; the hard part was everything around it. Ports needed giant cranes and vast storage yards. Railways and trucking firms needed matching equipment. Shipping lines had developed rival box sizes and corner fittings, so one company's containers would not fit another's cranes. Dockworkers' unions, understandably, resisted a technology that threatened most of their jobs.

Things accelerated once international standards for container dimensions and fittings were agreed in the late 1960s, which is why the industry still measures capacity in twenty-foot equivalent units. When any box could go on any ship, train or truck, the benefits snowballed. The huge American supply effort during the Vietnam War also gave container shipping a large, reliable customer at a crucial moment.

sections.heading: Winners, losers and a new map
sections.body:
Containerisation redrew the geography of trade. Historic waterfront ports in cramped city centres, such as Manhattan's piers and London's old docks, went into decline because they had no room for cranes and container yards, while new terminals sprang up on open land nearby, such as Port Newark–Elizabeth and Felixstowe. Dock employment collapsed in many cities, hollowing out working-class neighbourhoods that had depended on it for generations.

At the same time, cheap and predictable transport made it practical to spread manufacturing across continents. A phone or a car seat can contain parts from a dozen countries precisely because shipping a box of components halfway around the world costs very little compared with the value inside it. Global supply chains, and the rise of export-driven Asian economies, would have been far harder without it.

sections.heading: The lesson for innovators
sections.body:
The container story is a classic case of an innovation whose value lay almost entirely in standardisation and the surrounding system rather than in clever engineering. A steel box is trivial to build; persuading ports, carriers, unions and governments to reorganise around it took two decades.

Engineers in EV charging will recognise the pattern. A connector or a protocol is only as useful as its adoption across vendors, which is why open standards such as OCPP matter more than any single brilliant charger. The unglamorous work of agreeing interfaces is often where the real leverage lies.

lessons.takeaway: The shipping container changed the world not because the box was clever, but because everyone agreed to build around the same box. Standards and systems often matter more than inventions.

lessons.title: Never Split the Difference
lessons.author: Chris Voss
lessons.hook: A former FBI hostage negotiator argues that most business negotiations fail for the same reason kidnapping talks do: one side tries to win the argument instead of understanding the other. His toolkit is surprisingly gentle, and surprisingly effective.

sections.heading: From hostage talks to sales calls
sections.body:
Chris Voss spent years as the FBI's lead international kidnapping negotiator, and after leaving the bureau he began teaching negotiation to business students and executives. His central claim sounds almost heretical in a business school: people are not the rational calculators that classic negotiation theory assumes. Under pressure they are driven by fear, pride and the need to feel in control, and a negotiator who ignores emotions is ignoring most of the game.

That is also why he distrusts the idea of meeting halfway. Splitting the difference often produces a compromise that neither side really wanted, chosen mainly because it ends the discomfort of disagreeing. Voss would rather find out what the other party actually needs and build the deal around that.

sections.heading: Tactical empathy
sections.body:
The core of the method is what Voss calls tactical empathy: deliberately working out how the other side sees the situation and then saying it out loud. Empathy here is not agreement or sympathy. You can understand someone's position perfectly without conceding anything. The point is that people who feel understood stop defending themselves and start talking, and the more they talk, the more you learn.

Two simple tools do most of the work. Mirroring means repeating the last few words the other person said, with a slightly questioning tone, which nudges them to elaborate. Labelling means naming the emotion or concern you sense, for example: "It sounds like the delivery timeline is what really worries you." A well-chosen label defuses tension, and a wrong one costs little, because the other side will simply correct you, which is useful information too.

sections.heading: Why 'no' is a good start
sections.body:
Voss is sceptical of several pieces of sales folklore. Pushing someone towards an early "yes" tends to make them wary: they sense a trap and dig in. A "no", by contrast, makes people feel safe and in control, so it often opens the real conversation. Asking whether something would be a bad idea invites a comfortable no that actually moves things forward.

He also distinguishes between two kinds of agreement. "You're right" is frequently what people say just to end a discussion. The response worth aiming for is "that's right", which signals that the other side recognises its own view in your summary. Another technique is the accusation audit: before making a difficult proposal, list the negative things the other side probably thinks about you and say them first. This takes the sting out of their objections and makes you seem fair rather than defensive.

Behind all of these techniques lies one observation: people are far more afraid of losing something than they are excited about gaining something of equal value. Voss suggests framing your proposal around what the other side stands to lose by walking away, rather than around what they might gain, because a potential loss tends to concentrate the mind far more effectively.

sections.heading: Questions that hand the problem back
sections.body:
Instead of flatly rejecting an unreasonable demand, Voss recommends calibrated questions: open questions beginning with "how" or "what" that hand the problem back to the other side. Asking how a requested deadline could realistically be met forces the customer to engage with your constraints, without you ever having to refuse outright. Questions beginning with "why" are best avoided, because they tend to sound accusatory.

On price, he favours a structured approach: set an ambitious target, make a series of shrinking concessions, and finish on a precise, non-round number. An offer of 37,850 euros sounds like the result of careful calculation; 40,000 sounds like an opening bid waiting to be haggled down.

sections.heading: Using it at work
sections.body:
For anyone selling software to transit operators or negotiating scope with stakeholders, the main lesson is to slow down. Spend the first part of a tough meeting finding out what the other side fears, what constraints they face and who else must approve the deal. Label their worries, summarise until they agree with your summary, and only then talk about your offer.

None of this is manipulation if it is done honestly. At its best, the method is simply disciplined listening, and in most negotiations careful listening is a rarer and more valuable skill than clever arguing.

lessons.takeaway: Negotiation is less about winning arguments than about making the other side feel genuinely understood. Listen, label and ask how before you ever name your price.

lessons.hook: In 1900, nearly four in ten American cars were electric, and a century later we are still treating electric mobility as a novelty. The reason they disappeared has less to do with batteries than you might think.

quiz.question: What does the lesson suggest is the main parallel for charging software today?

sections.body:
In 1900, if you had stood on a busy street in New York, you would have been just as likely to see a car gliding along on batteries as one chugging along on petrol. Of the roughly 4,200 cars built in the United States that year, about 38 percent were electric, 40 percent were steam-powered and only 22 percent ran on gasoline. Electric cars were quiet, clean and needed no skill to start. In 1899 a Belgian electric car called La Jamais Contente had even become the first road vehicle to exceed 100 km/h.

Yet within about two decades the electric car had all but vanished. The popular story blames a single villain, but the truth is a chain of small shifts that reinforced one another. That is what makes the episode so instructive: nobody ever decided that electric would lose.
sections.heading: The forgotten head start

sections.body:
Start with the humble crank. Early petrol engines had to be started by hand, by swinging a heavy metal handle at the front of the car. If the engine backfired, the handle could kick back violently, and broken wrists and forearms were common enough to earn their own nickname: the chauffeur's fracture. Beyond the injuries, cranking a cold engine on a winter morning was a real ordeal, which is exactly why electric cars were marketed to doctors, city dwellers and many women drivers.

In 1911 Charles Kettering, working at Delco, developed a compact electric starter motor, and Cadillac fitted it to its 1912 models. Ironically, it was electricity that rescued the combustion engine. Overnight, the electric car's strongest selling point, 'no cranking, just go', became table stakes for everybody. A small motor and battery, an engineer's answer to a usability problem, had removed the petrol car's biggest handicap.
sections.heading: The arm-breaking problem

sections.body:
Then came the economics. Ford's Model T arrived in 1908, and once it was built on a moving assembly line from 1913, its price kept falling, eventually dropping below $300 in the mid-1920s. A typical electric roadster of 1912 cost around $1,750, roughly three times as much as a Model T. Heavy lead-acid batteries were expensive to build and to replace, so the electric car could not follow that price curve.

Fuel supply moved in the opposite direction. The gusher at Spindletop, Texas, in 1901 and the oil fields that followed made gasoline abundant and cheap, and you could buy it almost anywhere in a can. Electric cars were excellent for city errands of 50 to 80 km, but as roads improved and people wanted to travel between towns, the limited range became a serious weakness. In rural America, where most farms had no grid connection until well into the 1930s, an electric car simply could not be recharged.
sections.heading: Cheap oil and a cheaper car

sections.body: The deeper lesson is about feedback loops. Each advantage for petrol made the next one easier: more buyers meant bigger factories, lower prices, more filling stations and more mechanics, which in turn attracted still more buyers. Electric cars, serving a small niche, never crossed the threshold where that cycle could start. Detroit Electric kept building cars until 1939, but as a boutique brand for a loyal few. Today we would call this a network effect, and it explains why the technically elegant option does not always win. The option that is easiest to live with, at scale, usually does.
sections.heading: A feedback loop nobody planned

sections.body:
For anyone building charging software, the parallels are hard to miss. Drivers do not judge an EV by its kilowatt-hours; they judge the whole experience: finding a free charger, starting a session, paying, and trusting that it will actually work. Kettering's starter did not improve the engine at all. It removed friction. Reliable uptime, transparent pricing, roaming and plug-and-charge are today's starter motor.

So when you prioritise a backlog, remember that adoption often hinges on removing one stubborn annoyance rather than on a technical breakthrough. Ask not 'what is the most advanced feature we could add?' but 'what is our version of the hand crank?'
sections.heading: What it means for your roadmap

lessons.takeaway: Electric cars did not lose because the technology failed, but because petrol removed its biggest annoyance, got cheaper, and then fed on its own growth. Removing friction often matters more than adding features.

lessons.title: Why Europe runs on 50 Hz and America on 60 Hz
lessons.hook: The frequency humming in your walls was not chosen by physics. It was the outcome of a commercial race in the 1890s, and we are still living with the result.

sections.heading: A choice nobody planned
sections.body:
Early electric systems were a patchwork. Individual companies picked whatever frequency suited their generators and lamps, and in the 1880s one could find networks running anywhere from 25 to 133 cycles per second. There was no grand standard, only competing equipment catalogues.

Low frequencies made large rotating machines and long transmission lines easier to build, while higher frequencies stopped incandescent lamps from visibly flickering. Every engineer was juggling these trade-offs with incomplete knowledge.

sections.heading: Two manufacturers, two answers
sections.body:
In the United States, Westinghouse settled on 60 Hz around 1890, partly because it suited both lighting and the induction motors it was starting to sell. In Germany, AEG standardised on 50 Hz, a figure that fitted neatly into the metric preference for round numbers and the design of its generators.

Once a dominant supplier had committed, the rest of each market followed. Utilities bought compatible equipment, factories bought compatible motors, and the choice quickly became entrenched.

sections.heading: Path dependence in action
sections.body:
Economists call this path dependence: an early, somewhat arbitrary decision becomes locked in because switching later would be ruinously expensive. Japan is the most striking example. Tokyo bought German generators and Osaka bought American ones, so to this day the eastern half of the country runs at 50 Hz and the western half at 60 Hz, linked only by a handful of converter stations.

That split became painfully visible after the 2011 earthquake, when the east lost generating capacity and the west could send only a trickle of power across the frequency border.

sections.heading: Does the difference matter today?
sections.body:
For most consumer electronics, hardly at all, because switch-mode power supplies rectify the input anyway. For motors, transformers and grid equipment it still matters: a motor runs about twenty percent faster at 60 Hz, and transformer cores must be sized for the lower frequency.

For anyone designing charging infrastructure or exporting electrical equipment, the lesson is broader. Many 'technical' standards are historical accidents, and knowing their origin helps you judge which constraints are truly physical and which are merely inherited.

lessons.takeaway: 50 Hz and 60 Hz are the legacy of two manufacturers' commercial choices, locked in by path dependence rather than by any physical optimum.

lessons.title: The Goal
lessons.author: Eliyahu Goldratt
lessons.hook: A plant manager has ninety days to save his factory, and the answer turns out to be hiding in a single slow machine. The lesson applies to almost any system that has to deliver work.

sections.heading: A novel about throughput
sections.body:
Most management books lecture. Goldratt chose to tell a story instead: a factory manager called Alex Rogo is told that his plant will be closed unless it starts making money within three months. Everyone around him is busy, the machines are running flat out, and yet orders are late and inventory piles up in every corner.

The novel format is not a gimmick. It lets the reader watch a smart person cling to sensible-sounding beliefs and then slowly discard them, which is exactly how real organisations change their minds.

sections.heading: The bottleneck sets the pace
sections.body:
The central insight is deceptively simple. In any chain of dependent steps, the output of the whole system is governed by its slowest link, the constraint. An hour gained at a non-constraint is a mirage; an hour lost at the constraint is an hour lost for the entire plant.

This turns conventional efficiency thinking on its head. Keeping every machine and every person fully utilised feels responsible, but upstream of the bottleneck it only produces queues of half-finished work that tie up cash and hide problems.

sections.heading: Five focusing steps
sections.body:
Goldratt distils the method into a loop. Identify the constraint. Decide how to exploit it, so that it never sits idle or works on the wrong thing. Subordinate everything else to that decision. Only then elevate the constraint by adding capacity. Finally, go back to the start, because once one bottleneck is relieved another will emerge somewhere else.

The order matters. Teams love to jump straight to buying a new machine or hiring more people, when a surprising amount of capacity can usually be squeezed out of the existing constraint for free.

sections.heading: Why it matters beyond factories
sections.body:
Software teams, sales pipelines and charging depots all behave like production lines. If code review is the slowest step, writing more code faster simply lengthens the review queue. If a single grid connection limits a depot, clever scheduling around that connection beats adding chargers.

The practical habit is to ask, before optimising anything, whether it sits on the critical path. If it does not, the improvement may be real locally and still worthless for the system as a whole.

lessons.takeaway: Find the one step that limits the whole system and make every other decision serve it; local efficiency elsewhere is often an illusion.

vocab.definition: as fast or as hard as possible

vocab.definition: appearing easy while actually being subtle or difficult

quiz.question: According to the book, what determines the output of a whole system?

Its slowest step, the constraint
The number of people employed
The most expensive machine

quiz.question: What happens when you keep non-bottleneck resources fully utilised?

Costs fall automatically
Work-in-progress piles up in front of the constraint
The bottleneck disappears

Hiring more staff everywhere
Measuring every machine's utilisation

lessons.title: The Mom Test
lessons.author: Rob Fitzpatrick
lessons.hook: Everyone will tell you your idea is great, including your mother. This short book explains how to ask questions that even people who love you cannot lie about.

sections.heading: The problem with asking for opinions
sections.body:
When you describe your idea and ask whether people would use it, you are inviting polite fiction. Friends, colleagues and potential customers want to be supportive, so they offer compliments and hypothetical promises that cost them nothing.

Fitzpatrick's point is that the fault lies with the question, not with the people. If a conversation can be passed by being nice, it will be, and you will walk away with a false sense of validation.

sections.heading: Talk about their life, not your idea
sections.body:
The remedy is to steer the conversation towards concrete past behaviour. Instead of asking whether someone would pay for a tool, ask how they dealt with the problem last time, what it cost them, and what they have already tried.

Specifics are hard to fake. A person who has never looked for a solution is unlikely to buy yours, however enthusiastic they sound; someone who has cobbled together spreadsheets and workarounds is showing you genuine pain.

sections.heading: Spotting bad data
sections.body:
The book catalogues the usual suspects: compliments, generic claims about the future ('I would definitely use that'), and long wish lists of features. None of them are evidence. Treat them as noise and gently dig for the reason behind each request.

A useful signal of real interest is commitment. It might be time, such as agreeing to a follow-up meeting with their boss, reputation, such as introducing you to a colleague, or money, such as a pre-order. If nothing is put on the line, the meeting was probably just pleasant.

sections.heading: Keeping conversations casual
sections.body:
Fitzpatrick advises against formal interviews where possible. A relaxed chat at a conference or a quick call feels less like a sales pitch, and people are more candid when they do not feel they are being researched.

For a product owner this translates into a simple discipline: before writing a ticket, be able to point to a real customer story behind it, not merely a request someone voiced in a meeting.

lessons.takeaway: Ask about specific past behaviour and look for commitment; compliments and promises about the future are not evidence.

vocab.definition: something people say to be kind even though they know it is not quite true
vocab.example: Saying the meeting was useful was a polite fiction everyone accepted.

vocab.definition: to guide something in a particular direction
vocab.example: She steered the discussion back to the budget.

vocab.definition: made roughly or quickly from whatever was available
vocab.example: The prototype was cobbled together over a weekend.

vocab.definition: the people or things you would normally expect to be involved
vocab.example: Slow tests and flaky builds were the usual suspects behind the delays.

vocab.definition: at risk; offered as a real commitment
vocab.example: With a pilot contract, the customer finally put something on the line.

vocab.definition: open and honest, even when the truth is uncomfortable
vocab.example: Thanks for the candid feedback on the onboarding flow.

quiz.question: Why do people give misleading feedback on ideas, according to the book?
options: They want to steal the idea
They are being polite, and the question allows it
They don't understand technology
They are paid competitors
quiz.explanation: If a question can be passed by being nice, people will be nice.

quiz.question: Which question follows the book's advice best?
options: Would you pay for this app?
Do you like my idea?
How did you handle this problem the last time it happened?
What features should the app have?
quiz.explanation: Asking about concrete past behaviour produces evidence that is hard to fake.

quiz.question: What counts as a strong signal of real interest?
options: An enthusiastic compliment
A long feature wish list
A commitment of time, reputation or money
A promise to use it someday
quiz.explanation: Commitment means the person is putting something on the line.
